overview: This is the modern Republic of Kazakhstan, independent since 16 December 1991, not the earlier Kazakh Khanate or every steppe community. The atlas begins in 1994 and supplies three border snapshots ending in 2020, while leaving the country’s lifetime open. Its simplified Caspian coast even leaves the city of Aktau outside the outline. The map is not a legal boundary survey. Soviet-era examples below are clearly labeled inherited history; modern family practices vary across this diverse country.

periods.title: Independence and new institutions
periods.summary: Kazakhstan became independent during the breakup of the Soviet Union.

periods.title: The 1995 constitutional framework
periods.summary: Nursultan Nazarbayev headed the state as institutions developed under the 1995 Constitution.

periods.title: Presidential succession
periods.summary: Nazarbayev resigned in March 2019 and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev became president.

periods.title: Unrest and constitutional amendments
periods.summary: Deadly January unrest was followed by constitutional changes and elections whose competitiveness observers questioned.

periods.title: A new constitutional framework
periods.summary: The replacement Constitution entered into force on 1 July 2026; parliamentary elections followed in August.

items.text: Kazakhstan declared independence on 16 December 1991, before this atlas record starts. The new state inherited institutions and infrastructure from a Soviet republic while creating its own national government. Independence did not mean that the people or their cultures suddenly began in 1991; it changed sovereignty and the framework within which they lived.

The Constitution adopted in 1995 shaped a long period under President Nursultan Nazarbayev. He resigned on 19 March 2019, and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev addressed Parliament as president the next day. The official speech is evidence for the transfer, while its praise of the outgoing leader is the government’s own political presentation.

January 2022 brought unrest and deadly violence. Constitutional amendments followed that June, including the replacement of the Constitutional Council with a Constitutional Court and removal of the death penalty from the Constitution. OSCE observers nevertheless found that the November presidential election lacked genuine competition. Changing legal rules and changing how political power operates are related but different processes.

A new Constitution adopted at the March 2026 referendum entered into force on 1 July, replacing the 1995 text. Elections to the new Kurultai legislature followed on 23 August. In their preliminary assessment, international observers described technically prepared elections but limited political alternatives and concerns about vote counting. The new framework should therefore be described alongside evidence about its implementation.

A short Kazakh writing sample is Қазақстан Республикасының Конституциясы, “Constitution of the Republic of Kazakhstan.” An editorial Latin rendering is Qazaqstan Respublikasynyñ Konstitutsiyasy. These Cyrillic words head the official Kazakh text of the Constitution effective from July 2026. They demonstrate a specific modern written form, not the script of medieval steppe inscriptions or a claim that everyone in the country uses only one language.

The famine of 1930 to 1933 happened under Soviet rule, decades before independence. Historian Sarah Cameron’s research links the catastrophe to state campaigns that forced rural people into collective farms and factories and confiscated livestock; she estimates more than 1.5 million deaths. Russian- and Kazakh-language sources help recover this history. Remembering it today does not make the modern republic the government that caused it.

The Soviet Union conducted more than 450 nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk between 1949 and 1989. The test site closed on 29 August 1991, before Kazakhstan’s December independence. The country subsequently renounced the nuclear arsenal left on its territory. Kazakhstan also promoted the International Day Against Nuclear Tests on the closure anniversary. This is a history of stopping testing, not of an independent Kazakh nuclear-testing programme.

Diversion of rivers for irrigation helped shrink the Aral Sea during the Soviet era and afterwards. The 13-kilometre Kok-Aral Dike, completed in August 2005, helped retain water in the northern part. The World Bank’s 2008 account reported falling salinity and a fish harvest rising from about 50 tonnes in 2004 to about 2,000 in 2007. This was an important local recovery, not restoration of the entire sea.

Oil remains economically important, but national growth does not describe every household’s experience. The World Bank’s February 2026 update linked strong 2025 output growth partly to higher oil production, while noting falling real incomes and consumption supported by borrowing. A busier economy and a family struggling with prices can exist at the same time.

Baikonur connects several political eras. The Soviet launch centre sent up Sputnik in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin in 1961. After the Soviet Union dissolved, Russia leased the site from independent Kazakhstan. Those famous early flights were Soviet achievements on this territory; they should not be relabeled inventions of a state founded thirty years later.

On 2 September 2015, Kazakh cosmonaut Aidyn Aimbetov launched from Baikonur with Sergey Volkov of Russia’s space agency and Andreas Mogensen of the European Space Agency on a mission to the International Space Station. NASA confirmed that all three reached orbit. Just before liftoff, the station itself had passed over Kazakhstan: the destination was already racing overhead while the crew prepared to chase it.

sections.title: Family gatherings, food and a dancing goat

items.text: UNESCO’s 2024 account of betashar describes a wedding welcome built around song and the unveiling of the bride. A singer names relatives, the bride and her sisters-in-law greet them with bows, and the groom’s mother welcomes her into the family. Relatives shower the newlyweds with sweets and coins. Elders pass on the practice; it is one documented Kazakh tradition, not a rule followed by every household.

In orteke, a musician plays a two-string dombyra while strings from their fingers move a wooden mountain-goat puppet. The goat taps and hops on a drum surface in time with the music. Some experts manage three or more puppets. That is a concert and a tiny goat dance party run by the same pair of hands. UNESCO inscribed this performing art in 2022.

A cooking competition at the Kokshetau cultural centre brought ten local enterprises together to make Nauryz kozhe, a festive dish associated with the spring celebration. The regional account describes a seven-ingredient version with water, meat, barley, kefir, kurt, salt and herbs. Judges considered presentation as well as taste. The accompanying display included quilting, weaving and felt work: plenty to look at between spoonfuls.

UNESCO describes orteke as a way for adults and children to communicate as well as entertain each other. Skills pass through communities and apprenticeships, with festivals and competitions helping performers learn from neighbours. Musical education can happen through watching hands, listening carefully and trying again, as well as through written lessons.

sections.title: Learning, care and the practical business of water

items.text: In 2022, seventeen-year-old Amina Pusurmanova joined the UniSat programme in Almaty. Participants designed cases, saw their designs printed in 3D, assembled devices and learned from teammates across Central Asia. Amina described Uzbek participants helping her use circuit-design software. The devices flew into the stratosphere that March, not into orbit. Learning science also meant asking a new friend for help.

A 2023 UNICEF report follows home-visiting nurse Aizharkyn in Zhetysay. Her work includes looking at a baby’s feeding and development, the family’s living conditions and possible dangers, then referring children to specialists when needed. She also attended emergency-preparedness training. Care here travels to the household and considers how a child lives, rather than stopping at a clinic doorway.

Astana hosted the Global Conference on Primary Health Care in October 2018. Its declaration renewed an international commitment to accessible community-based care and recalled the 1978 Alma-Ata declaration, made when Kazakhstan was a Soviet republic. Hosting an agreement is a diplomatic and public-health contribution; it does not by itself prove that every family can obtain the care it needs.

School toilets became a public issue, not just a caretaker’s problem. WHO’s 2024 account describes an assessment of 153 schools and collaboration between campaigners, ministries and specialists. A national standard effective that January set requirements linked to pupil numbers and included children with additional needs. A toilet must be usable by the children actually attending the school; adopting a standard is only one step towards that result.

ending.text: Kazakhstan remains a continuing state. The atlas’s last border interval ends in 2020 because of data coverage, not national collapse. The 2026 Constitution and parliamentary election mark institutional change within the same republic; observers’ concerns about political competition show why legal changes require continuing scrutiny. Communities, family practices and public services have their own histories within that ongoing political story.
